title: Clocks in the Earth: Radiocarbon and the Dating of the Past
titleCn: 地下的时钟：放射性碳与考古测年

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Until the middle of the twentieth century, archaeologists faced a frustrating limitation. They could often establish the order in which things had happened, but rarely how long ago. The principle of stratigraphy, according to which deeper layers of soil are generally older than those above them, allowed excavators to arrange finds in sequence, and changes in the style of pottery or tools could be used to link one site with another. Absolute dates, however, depended almost entirely on connections with societies that had kept written records, above all ancient Egypt. For prehistoric Europe, where no such records existed, chronologies were built on chains of comparison stretching across thousands of kilometres, and a single weak link could distort the whole structure.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The method that broke this dependence was developed in the late 1940s by the American chemist Willard Libby, who later received a Nobel Prize for the work. It rests on a simple principle. Cosmic rays striking the upper atmosphere produce small quantities of a radioactive form of carbon, carbon-14, which mixes with ordinary carbon and is taken up by plants through photosynthesis and by the animals that eat them. While an organism is alive, its proportion of carbon-14 remains roughly constant, but at death the intake stops and the carbon-14 already present begins to decay at a known rate, with half of it disappearing in about 5,700 years. By measuring how much remains in a piece of bone, wood or charcoal, scientists can estimate when the organism died.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Libby tested his method on materials whose age was already known, including timber from Egyptian tombs, and the results were close enough to the historical dates to inspire confidence. Within two decades, laboratories around the world were producing thousands of dates. It soon became apparent, however, that the method rested on an assumption that was not quite correct. Libby had supposed that the amount of carbon-14 in the atmosphere had remained constant over time. Careful comparisons revealed that it had in fact fluctuated, as a result of changes in solar activity and in the Earth's magnetic field, so that a raw radiocarbon measurement could not be converted directly into a calendar date.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The solution came from trees. Because many species add one growth ring each year, a sequence of rings can be counted back from the present, and by matching patterns of wide and narrow rings in overlapping timbers, researchers have built continuous records extending back thousands of years. Measuring the carbon-14 in rings of known age allowed scientists to construct a calibration curve that translates radiocarbon results into calendar years. The long-lived bristlecone pines of the American south-west, some of them several thousand years old, played a central part in establishing the early sections of this curve. The effect on prehistoric chronology was dramatic: for some periods, calibrated dates turned out to be several centuries older than the raw figures had suggested.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This recalibration, sometimes described as the second radiocarbon revolution, had consequences that went well beyond technical detail. Many archaeologists had assumed that major innovations, from metalworking to monumental architecture, had reached Europe from the older civilisations of the Near East. Once the dates were corrected, some of the great stone tombs of western Europe turned out to be older than the Egyptian pyramids, which therefore could hardly have inspired them. One influential archaeologist argued in the 1970s that the traditional picture of prehistoric Europe as a passive receiver of ideas from the east would have to be abandoned. Not every element of his argument has survived, but its broad conclusion is now widely accepted.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Radiocarbon dating is nevertheless far from infallible. Samples can be contaminated by younger carbon from groundwater or plant roots, or by modern material introduced during excavation and storage. A more subtle difficulty arises with wood. The rings at the centre of a tree may be centuries older than those at its edge, so charcoal from a long-lived tree may give a date well before the fire in which it was burned. Human activity has also complicated matters: the burning of fossil fuels, which contain no carbon-14, has diluted the atmosphere's supply, while nuclear weapons tests in the 1950s and 1960s temporarily almost doubled it. Forensic scientists, ironically, have found a use for this sudden rise, since it allows recent organic material to be dated with considerable precision.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Technical advances have reduced some of these problems. From the late 1970s, a technique known as accelerator mass spectrometry made it possible to count carbon-14 atoms directly instead of waiting for them to decay, so that samples of a few milligrams could be dated where several grams had previously been needed. A single seed or a tiny fragment of bone can now be analysed without destroying an entire object. Statistical methods also allow dates from a site to be combined with information about the order of the layers, sometimes narrowing the probable age of an event to a few decades. Even so, every radiocarbon date is a range of probabilities rather than a precise point, and archaeologists who forget this risk building new chronologies on foundations almost as fragile as the old ones.

title: The Gentle Push: What Nudges Can and Cannot Do
titleCn: 温和的推力：「助推」能做到什么、做不到什么

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, economic theory rested on a convenient simplification: that people, when making choices, weigh the available options carefully and select the one that best serves their interests. Few economists believed that real individuals behaved exactly like this, but the assumption made the mathematics manageable, and it implied that the most reliable way to change behaviour was to change incentives, through prices, taxes or penalties. From the 1970s onwards, however, a number of psychologists began to document systematic ways in which human decisions depart from this model. People, they showed, are swayed by the way information is presented, give more weight to losses than to equivalent gains, and tend to stick with whatever option requires no action on their part.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: These findings reached a wide audience in 2008 through a popular book written by an American economist and a legal scholar. Its central claim was that, since every decision is made in some context, those who design that context, whom the authors called 'choice architects', inevitably influence the outcome. Rather than pretend otherwise, governments and organisations should arrange choices so that people are gently steered towards options that they themselves would probably judge to be good for them. Crucially, such a 'nudge' must leave every option open and must not significantly change the costs involved: placing fruit at eye level in a school canteen counts as a nudge, whereas banning sweets does not.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The most frequently cited success concerns saving for retirement. When employees have to sign up for a workplace pension, many never get round to doing so, even though they say they intend to. When they are enrolled automatically and must actively choose to leave, participation rises dramatically. After the United Kingdom made automatic enrolment a legal requirement for employers in the 2010s, the proportion of eligible private-sector employees saving into a pension increased from well under half to the great majority. Similar effects have been reported for organ donation, where countries that presume consent unless people opt out often record far higher registration rates than those in which donors must actively sign up, although the number of actual donations depends on many other factors.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Encouraged by such results, governments in many countries established specialist teams to apply behavioural insights to public policy. The British team, set up in 2010, became one of the best known. Among its trials were letters to people who had not paid their taxes, which stated that most people in their area had already paid; this single sentence, appealing to the desire to conform, measurably increased payment rates. Because changes of this kind cost almost nothing to implement, even small improvements could represent excellent value for money, and the approach appealed to politicians of very different views.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: From the beginning, however, nudging attracted criticism. Some objections were ethical. If the effectiveness of a nudge depends on people not noticing it, critics asked, is it not a form of manipulation, however good the intentions behind it? And who decides which options people would choose if they were thinking clearly? Defenders replied that there is no neutral way to present choices, so the alternative to deliberate design is not freedom but accidental influence. This answer is persuasive as far as it goes, but it does not settle the question of who should be trusted to act as the architect, or how their decisions can be scrutinised.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Other objections concern the evidence. The early literature was dominated by striking results, and there is good reason to think that studies with impressive findings were more likely to be published than those that found little or nothing. When researchers compared the trials reported in academic journals with the full set of trials carried out by government nudge units, which had to record every result, they found that the average effect in the latter was considerably smaller. Some well-known findings have also failed to reappear when experiments were repeated. None of this means that nudges do not work, but it suggests that their typical impact is modest, often a matter of a few percentage points.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most serious concern is that nudges may be used as a substitute for policies that would be more effective but politically harder. Encouraging individuals to eat more healthily or to reduce their energy use is cheaper and less controversial than taxing unhealthy food or regulating polluting industries, but it is unlikely to achieve as much. Nudges are best understood as a useful addition to the tools of government, valuable precisely because they are cheap, rather than as an alternative to the difficult decisions that serious problems require. Used in that spirit, the gentle push has earned its place; treated as a solution in itself, it risks becoming an excuse for doing very little.

title: Concrete: An Ancient Material with a Modern Problem
titleCn: 混凝土：古老材料的现代难题

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Concrete is so common that it has become almost invisible. It forms the foundations of houses, the decks of bridges, the walls of dams and the floors of most modern buildings, and by some estimates it is the most widely used material on Earth after water. Its basic recipe is simple: sand and gravel, known as aggregate, are bound together by cement, which reacts chemically with water to form a hard, stone-like mass. Contrary to popular belief, concrete does not set by drying out. The reaction, called hydration, continues for months or even years, which is why freshly poured concrete is often kept damp rather than allowed to dry.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The Romans were not the first to use materials of this kind, but they used them on a scale and with a skill that would not be matched for well over a thousand years. Their cement combined lime with volcanic ash from the area around the Bay of Naples, and with it they built aqueducts, harbours and, most famously, the dome of the Pantheon in Rome. Completed in the second century AD, the dome remains the largest ever built of unreinforced concrete. Roman sea walls, constantly washed by salt water, have survived for around two thousand years, and recent research suggests that the seawater itself reacted with the volcanic ash to form new minerals that made the material stronger over time.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: After the collapse of the Western Roman Empire, the use of concrete declined sharply in Europe, and builders returned largely to stone, brick and timber. Interest revived in the eighteenth century, when engineers began to experiment with cements that would set under water, and in 1824 an English bricklayer named Joseph Aspdin patented a product he called Portland cement, because he thought the hardened material resembled a well-known building stone quarried on the Isle of Portland. Later manufacturers greatly improved the process, heating mixtures of limestone and clay to much higher temperatures, but the name survived, and Portland cement remains the basis of almost all concrete produced today.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Concrete has one important weakness: although it is extremely strong when compressed, it cracks easily when stretched or bent. In the second half of the nineteenth century, several inventors, among them a French gardener who wanted stronger flowerpots, found that embedding iron or steel within concrete solved this problem, since the metal resists the tension that the concrete cannot. The combination works partly because steel and concrete expand and contract by almost the same amount as temperatures change, so they do not tear apart in hot or cold weather. Reinforced concrete made possible the long bridges, tall buildings and thin curved roofs of the twentieth century.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Yet reinforcement introduced a new vulnerability. Concrete is slightly porous, and over time water and salts can penetrate it and reach the steel. When steel rusts, it expands, and the pressure this creates breaks the surrounding concrete from within, exposing more metal to attack. This process is a particular problem for bridges and car parks in countries where salt is spread on roads in winter. Many reinforced concrete structures are designed to last between fifty and a hundred years, far less than the Roman buildings that have stood for two millennia, and the cost of repairing or replacing the large stock of structures built in the mid-twentieth century is becoming a major burden for governments.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The most pressing problem, however, is the effect of cement on the climate. Cement production is responsible for around eight per cent of the world's carbon dioxide emissions, more than the entire aviation industry. Part of this comes from burning fuel to heat kilns to around 1,450 degrees Celsius, but the larger share is released by the chemical reaction itself: when limestone is heated, it breaks down and gives off carbon dioxide. This means that even if kilns were powered entirely by clean energy, the manufacture of conventional cement would still produce large quantities of the gas. Demand, meanwhile, continues to grow, driven by rapid urbanisation in Asia and Africa.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Engineers are pursuing several ways of reducing this impact. One is to replace part of the cement with other materials, such as ash from coal-fired power stations or slag left over from steel production, both of which can react in a similar way. The supply of these by-products is limited, however, and will shrink further as coal power is phased out, so attention has turned to clays that can be treated to perform a similar role. Other approaches involve capturing the carbon dioxide released at cement plants, or injecting it into fresh concrete, where it is locked away as a mineral. Perhaps the simplest solution is to use less concrete in the first place, through more careful design, although this requires changes in an industry that has long favoured generous safety margins over economy of material.

title: The Garden City: A Radical Idea and Its Uneven Legacy
titleCn: 田园城市：一个激进构想及其参差的遗产

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: At the end of the nineteenth century, the great industrial cities of Britain presented a grim picture. Overcrowded housing, polluted air and high rents drove reformers to search for alternatives, while the countryside, emptied by the decline of agriculture, offered fresh air but few jobs and little social life. Into this debate stepped an unlikely figure. Ebenezer Howard was a London stenographer who earned his living recording speeches and legal proceedings, and he had no training in architecture or planning. In 1898 he published a short book, reissued four years later under the title 'Garden Cities of To-morrow', which proposed nothing less than a new way of organising the relationship between town and country.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Howard illustrated his argument with a famous diagram of three magnets. The town attracted people with jobs, wages and entertainment, but repelled them with crowding and dirt; the country offered beauty and clean air, but little work or amusement. A third magnet, the 'town-country', would combine the advantages of both. In practical terms, he proposed new settlements of around 32,000 people, built on land bought cheaply in agricultural areas. Each town would be surrounded by a permanent belt of farmland, which would supply it with food and prevent it from expanding. When one town reached its planned size, another would be founded nearby, and the towns would be connected by rail to form a cluster.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The physical layout, however, was only part of the scheme, and in Howard's eyes probably not the most important part. The land on which each garden city stood was to be owned collectively, through a trust, rather than by private landlords. As the town grew and the land became more valuable, the increase in its value would therefore benefit the community, paying off the original loans and then funding schools, parks and pensions. Howard regarded this as a peaceful path to social reform, one that would achieve many of the aims of radical politics without taking anyone's property away from them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Remarkably, Howard's ideas were put into practice within his lifetime. A company was formed to buy land in Hertfordshire, north of London, and work on Letchworth Garden City began in 1903; a second town, Welwyn Garden City, followed in 1920. Both were designed with generous gardens, tree-lined streets and a clear separation between housing and industry. Neither grew as quickly as Howard had hoped, and financial pressures forced the companies that developed them to compromise on some of his principles. Nevertheless, in Letchworth a community foundation still owns a substantial part of the town's land and property and spends the income on local services, a partial realisation of his original vision.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The influence of the garden city movement spread far beyond these two towns. In Britain, the new towns built after the Second World War, such as Stevenage, drew heavily on Howard's ideas, as did the green belts that were drawn around London and other cities to restrict their growth. Abroad, planners from Germany to Japan adopted elements of the model, and the term 'garden city' was applied to developments on several continents. Yet in most cases what was copied was the appearance of Howard's towns, with their low-density housing and abundant greenery, rather than the system of collective land ownership on which he believed their success depended.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This selective borrowing helps to explain why the garden city has attracted so much criticism. Many developments that claimed to follow Howard's model were in fact suburbs without industries of their own, from which residents travelled daily to work in the city. Once cars became widespread, such low-density estates encouraged long journeys and contributed to the spread of building across the countryside, the very outcome Howard had hoped to prevent. Some urban thinkers went further, arguing in the 1960s that his entire approach was hostile to the variety and liveliness of real cities. These criticisms have some force, but they are directed more at the imitations than at the original proposal.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Interest in Howard has revived in recent years, as governments facing housing shortages have announced plans for new 'garden towns' and 'garden villages'. Whether these deserve the name is open to question. Most adopt the green spaces and attractive streets, but few include any mechanism for capturing the rising value of land for the community. Yet this was the most original element of Howard's thinking, and arguably the most relevant today, when the profits from turning farmland into building land usually go to landowners and developers. A genuine revival of the garden city would need to begin not with the design of houses, but with the question of who owns the ground beneath them.

title: Too Late to Learn? Age and the Acquisition of Language
titleCn: 学语言会太晚吗？年龄与语言习得

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Almost every child acquires the language spoken around them without formal instruction, and by the age of four or five most have mastered its basic grammar. Adults learning a new language, by contrast, often struggle for years and rarely lose their foreign accent. Observations like these have given rise to one of the most widely held beliefs about language: that there is a limited window in childhood during which languages can be learned with ease, and that once it closes, full mastery becomes difficult or impossible. The belief influences decisions made by parents and governments alike, yet the scientific evidence behind it is more complicated than its popularity suggests.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The idea was given its classic form in the 1960s by a neurologist who proposed that the brain's capacity for language declines around puberty, as it loses the flexibility of early childhood. He called this the critical period, and he supported it partly by noting that children who suffer damage to the brain often recover their language far more completely than adults with similar injuries. Some of the most frequently cited evidence, however, has come from rare and tragic cases of children who were raised in severe isolation and who, when discovered, never fully acquired grammar despite intensive teaching. Such cases are deeply troubling, but they are of limited scientific value: the children concerned had suffered extreme neglect, so it is impossible to separate the effects of late exposure to language from those of their wider experiences.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: More persuasive evidence comes from deaf children born to hearing parents, some of whom are not exposed to sign language until later in childhood. Studies have found that those who begin signing early generally achieve greater control of grammar than those who begin as teenagers, even after decades of use. Research on infants points in a similar direction. At birth, babies can distinguish between speech sounds used in any of the world's languages, but by around their first birthday they have become much less sensitive to differences that do not matter in the language they hear around them. Infants raised in a Japanese-speaking environment, for instance, gradually lose the ability to hear the contrast between English 'r' and 'l'.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The picture for second languages is less clear. Studies of immigrants have repeatedly found that those who arrived as young children are more likely to sound like native speakers than those who arrived as adults, and accent appears to be the area in which age matters most. For grammar, the evidence is more mixed. One large online study, in which hundreds of thousands of participants completed a grammar quiz, suggested that the ability to learn grammar remains strong until about the age of seventeen or eighteen, far later than the traditional account would predict. Its authors noted, however, that reaching a native-like level still appears to require starting much earlier, because learning takes many years.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Moreover, in the early stages of learning, younger is not necessarily better. Experiments comparing learners of different ages in the same conditions have often found that adolescents and adults make faster initial progress than young children, probably because they can draw on more developed memory, greater knowledge of the world and the ability to think consciously about rules. Children tend to catch up with and overtake older learners only after several years of extensive exposure, when their capacity to absorb the language without conscious effort begins to show its advantages.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This matters a great deal for education policy. Many countries have lowered the age at which foreign languages are introduced at school, often on the assumption that an earlier start will automatically lead to better results. But a child who studies a language for two hours a week is in a very different position from one who is surrounded by it all day. Research comparing pupils who started a foreign language at school at different ages has generally found that, after the same number of hours of teaching, the later starters perform at least as well, and often better. Without substantial exposure, the advantage of youth appears to be small or absent.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Most researchers now prefer to speak of a sensitive period rather than a critical one, a phase in which the brain is especially responsive to language but whose end is gradual rather than sudden. Age is undoubtedly one factor in success, but it interacts with others, including the amount and quality of input, the learner's motivation and the opportunities available to use the language in real situations. For adults, the message is encouraging: native-like pronunciation may be out of reach for most, but high levels of competence are not. For schools, an early start is worthwhile only if it comes with enough time and good teaching to make use of it.
